0.0.n: Sets the season for the whole sentence.

0.2.n: Combines with 月 to name the third month, March.

0.3.n: After 3, this forms the month name March.

0.4.n: Marks March as the time reached in 3月になる.

0.5.n: With a month and に, なる describes the calendar reaching that month.

0.6.n: After なる, と introduces what regularly happens when March arrives.

0.8.n: Here, school refers to the school year coming to an end.

0.9.n: Marks 学校 as what comes to an end.

0.10.n: Gives the duration of the school period that is ending.

0.11.n: The connecting form of 終わる links the school year's end to the next statement.

0.13.n: Combines 卒業, graduation, with 式, ceremony.

0.14.n: Links 卒業式 to シーズン, specifying what kind of season it is.

0.15.n: An English loanword used here for the period when graduation ceremonies happen.

0.16.n: Politely completes the statement after the noun シーズン.

1.0.n: The speaker repeats the topic before giving an English-based explanation.

1.2.n: An English loanword offered as an explanation of 卒業式.

1.3.n: Invites the listener to recognize or agree with the explanation.

1.5.n: Refers here to schooling coming to an end before starting work.

1.6.n: Marks 学校 as what finishes.

1.7.n: The て-form of 終わる connects finishing school with starting work.

1.8.n: Used with 始める to describe beginning employment.

1.9.n: Marks 仕事 as what someone starts.

1.10.n: The plain form describes beginning work; the person doing it is left unstated.

2.0.n: Introduces another situation that involves graduating.

2.1.n: Names the school stage before 高校 in Japan.

2.2.n: Marks 中学校 as the stage that finishes.

2.3.n: The て-form of 終わる links completing junior high with moving on to high school.

2.4.n: A common shortened form of 高等学校.

2.5.n: Marks 高校 as the destination or next educational stage.

2.6.n: Here, 進む describes advancing to the next stage of education.

3.0.n: A polite connector presenting the next statement as a consequence.

3.1.n: The conditional form of 卒業する uses すれば to mean if or once graduation happens.

3.3.n: Combines with まで to set the endpoint of the period being discussed.

3.4.n: After 今, it forms 今まで, referring to the period up to now.

3.5.n: An unfinished start of 仲良かった; the speaker stops and restarts the word.

3.7.n: A casual past form of 仲良い, with が omitted from 仲が良かった; it describes 友達.

3.8.n: Described by the preceding phrase as people the speaker or listener was close with.

3.9.n: Marks 友達 as the people one would meet, using に with 会う.

3.10.n: From 会える, can meet; its negative linking form joins なる to describe losing that ability.

3.11.n: The polite form of なる completes 会えなくなる, describing a change to being unable to meet.

4.0.n: Modifies 先生 through の to identify which teachers are meant.

4.1.n: Links 学校 and 先生, showing the teachers' connection to the school.

4.2.n: Japanese does not mark plural here; the context suggests teachers as a group.

4.3.n: Combines と, marking whom one parts from, with も, adding teachers alongside friends.

4.4.n: The noun 別れ has the polite prefix お and refers to saying goodbye.

4.5.n: Politely ends the statement after the noun お別れ.

0.lit: Spring, when it becomes March, school ends for one year, and it is graduation ceremony season.
0.tip: A plain verb followed by と can introduce a predictable result, such as what happens every March.

1.lit: Graduation ceremony, graduation, right. School finishes, and one starts work.
1.tip: 終わって links two events in sequence: finishing school and then starting work.

2.lit: For example, junior high school finishes, and one advances to high school.
2.tip: に marks the destination in 高校に進む, even though the movement is educational rather than physical.

3.lit: Therefore, if you graduate, you become unable to meet friends you were clo... close with until now.
3.tip: A negative form ending in なく plus なる describes becoming unable to do something or no longer doing it.

4.lit: With school teachers too, it is parting.
4.tip: とも here is two particles together: と marks the people you part from, and も adds them too.
